utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. Today we are Wednesday, the 7th of November, 2007. I would like to greet the representative of the Prosecution, Mrs. Dahl, Mr. Seselj, as well as all the people assisting us in the courtroom, the registrar, the usher, the Legal Officer, as well as the interpreters, and the security guards. As you know, today this hearing will be dedicated to the opening statement of the Prosecution, but prior to that the Trial Chamber will hand down an oral decision on the issue of witness lists. I shall read this out slowly. Oral decision on the application filed -- on the application for reconsideration filed by the Prosecution of the decision relating to the adoption of protection measures on the 30th of October, 2007. Given the oral application filed by the Prosecution during the Pre-Trial Conference yesterday, with a view to asking for the reconsideration of the decision on the reconsideration by the Prosecution of the decision relating to the adoption of protective measures on the 30th of August, 2007, which had been handed down by the Pre-Trial Judge on the 16th of October, 2007, on a confidential basis. Given that the Prosecution yesterday asked for the late disclosure of 30 days before the beginning of trial be calculated on the basis of 30 days that should run after the testimony of the first witness following the winter recess at the end of the year and not 30 days before the testimony of the first witness which had been decided on the 16th of October, 2007. Considering the oral motion filed yesterday by the accused during the Pre-Trial Conference and with a -- with a view to asking that this be disclosed before the opening statement of the Prosecution the identity of all the witnesses which the Prosecution intends to call to testify, including those witnesses which have been granted late disclosure 30 days before their testimony considering the motion filed by the Prosecution, the Trial Chamber feels that there have been no change in circumstances or clear mistake which would justify the Trial Chamber changing or reconsidering its view. Considering this, the Trial Chamber would like to state once again that late disclosure of identity of witnesses was only granted in seven cases, and once the Pre-Trial Chamber reckoned it was absolutely necessary to protect the security of the witnesses in question whilst respecting the rights of the Defence. Considering that the Trial Chamber states that Rule 69(C) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence provides for nondisclosure of identity but that the latter should nonetheless be disclosed before the commencement of trial and in a deadline which entitles the Defence to prepare itself. But the case-law of this Tribunal has interpreted Rule 69(C) of the Rules as follows: This would entitle late disclosure of the identity to the accused only after the commencement of trial, insofar as these time limit entitles the Defence to prepare itself adequately. Let me repeat this. So long as the Defence is able to prepare itself properly. Considering that the accused has not demonstrate any change of circumstance or obvious error which would justify the Trial Chamber changing its view on those decisions taken on the 30th of August and 16th of October, therefore pursuant to Rule 69 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, orders that the October decision -- following the October decision and which granted late disclosure to seven witnesses, the Prosecution will communicate or disclose the identity of those witnesses at least 30 days before the 11th of December, 2007, this is when the Prosecution will call its first witness. Refer to the Scheduling Order of the 6th of 11. Considering that those decisions of the 16th of October and 12th of October have granted late disclosure of identity of witnesses 30 days before the testimony of certain witnesses, the Trial Chamber wishes this to be maintained. So much for the decision we have taken which I'll sum up. Therefore, the Trial Chamber maintains all its previous decision, which means the Prosecution will disclose the identity, not the list of witnesses that Mr. Seselj has already been provided with 30 days before the 11th of December, 2007, i.e., in a few days' time. On the 11th of December, 2007, the list of witnesses of protected witnesses, with the exception of those seven witnesses which have been granted protective measures, and stating that the disclosure of their identity will only be provided 30 days before they come to testify in this courtroom. That said, I shall now give the floor to Mrs. Dahl so that she can - just a minute, Mr. Seselj. I shall give you the floor in a few minutes - so that she can make her opening statement. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you have delivered the oral decision of the Trial Chamber on a very important question, I request orally to be allowed to appeal that decision because it considerably restricts my procedural rights guaranteed by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and this impedes the regularity of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we reckon that you have filed an oral motion with a view to certifying on appeal the decision that has just been handed down by this Trial Chamber. This Trial Chamber will rule on this. Now, Mrs. Dahl, you have four hours. If you will -- can finish at 1.30, all the better.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: May it please the Court. By 1993 thousands of civilians in the Balkans had been killed, thousands more were detained, beaten, and ultimately expelled, their homes and cultures destroyed. One witness who will come to tell the world what happened to her exemplifies the suffering of those inflicted by those bent on creating a larger state dominated by Serbs. This woman will testify that she lived in a town in Bosnia with her husband, two young children. She had very little political awareness. She was happy taking care of her children, she was nursing an infant, and she began to hear rumours of war. She lived in a mixed ethnic city. There were Serbs, Croats, and Muslims who lived peacefully together. She did not identify herself with her religious group nor did she choose her friends based on their ethnicity. She lived in a middle-class neighbourhood. There were rich people, poor people, like any normal city. During the elections, chaos began. Television and media were pulling the ethnic groups in all nationalist directions. People were calling out to stick together with their own ethnic groups. Serbs voted for one party, Muslims another, Croats for their own. When the elections were over, she noticed that her Serb neighbours started to move away. At first they told her they were just moving -- going away for a few days, but it became obvious that they were leaving permanently. She said the intellectuals were the first to flee, and they convinced the general Serb population to leave too. The Croats in her neighbourhood were quiet, people retreated to their own homes, people began sticking to themselves and avoiding the political mess. Older people, those who had survived the prior wars that had wracked the Balkans began to prepare for war. When the conflict in Croatia started, people in her neighbourhood still seemed to be getting along. Serb military reserves began to arrive in her city in late 1991 and early 1992. They wore military uniforms and drove around intimidating people. It was well-known that conflicts were breaking out. By April 1992, the Serbs had fled from her city and there were no more Croats or Muslims in the military barracks in her town; they had been replaced by Serbs. People were afraid in her city. People were hiding in their houses, they didn't dare come out. There were isolated killings. She heard of people being taken away from their houses. There were violent rumours everywhere. People kept their children home from school. She talked about what to do with her husband. They decided that maybe they would move to a relative's house in a nearby village. This relative had told her that things were still calm there. She moved her two children and her husband there. They stayed for several weeks. The house was overcrowded, they ran out of food. They tried to figure out what to do. Concerned for the safety of her two babies, they talked about going to Croatia. They arranged this plan, but this woman was afraid to leave her husband behind. She was afraid she would never see him again. They decided to stay together as a family and go to another nearby village where her mother-in-law said the Serbs were still treating the Muslims in a kind way. Her mother-in-law thought that they would be safe. She says now that going to this village was the worst decision she ever made in her life. Only she survived. In April 4, 1992, major military attacks began on her town. She and her two small children and other relatives who could fit into their car fled. They travelled in a mountainous region and then hid, trying to get to her mother-in-law's village. She's nursing an infant and has another child that needs to be carried. They got through a check-point manned by Serb police. They were polite, gave proper directions on how to get to her mother-in-law's village. This experience reassured her that everything was okay, that they would be safe. Unfortunately, this village was completely Muslim, and I say "unfortunately" because that made them a target for ethnic cleansing. The situation deteriorated in June 1992. They began to hear horrifying rumours of death and destruction. They were in a small village and they began to panic. She realised that it was perhaps too late to flee any further. They stayed in shelters, tried to dig trenches to give themselves a place to hide, nearby villages were shelled with artillery. They decided to go into the mountains, and in a group of about 200 people began to walk on foot. They saw that the village they left, which they had returned to at night, had been destroyed, leveled, burned. They tried to gather what clothes they could find and supplies. As they walked through the mountains looking for some safety, they left behind the belongings, realising that they were slowing them down. It became a problem that they were travelling with a large group of elderly people. The old people said, Leave us behind, save yourselves. Parents were aware of the danger, they were trying to shield their children. The grandparents said, Save our grandchildren. They left behind 16 elderly people. This woman found out that these 16 elderly people were killed, the bodies left out to rot. When they moved deeper into the mountains, they were completely lost. They had no food or water; because they were so high in the mountains, they found snow to melt and drink. They grew more and more exhausted. Shells fell, exploding, creating panic and confusion. This caused the group to panic, it divided into two. One-half of that group survived the war, they made it to safety. The group where our witness remained with her children and her husband and other family members went back toward their town, that by then had been captured by Serb Chetniks. Seven well-armed Serbs asked them to surrender. This small group of terrified and exhausted civilians thought that if they surrendered without any resistance, they would not be harmed. Some of the men had pistols, which they threw to the ground, but they were arrested and taken to another small village nearby. And as this witness will tell you, that's when the horror started. When I first read this witness's statement, I couldn't imagine anything worse, but indeed it got worse. That was the moment that they separated the men from the women and children. In their group, there were 29 men and 20 children. Most of the children were preschool age. There was even a seven-day-old baby. They were taken to a school. The women and children were placed on one side of the road and the men on another. Her husband was taken away by a man in a Serb uniform. Other members of the Serb military started to insult them, threaten them with rape, tell them how they would slaughter them and their children. They were herded like cattle. There was so much fear and hatred in their eyes, she was afraid that if the military came close they would have skinned them alive. At one point she asked a Serb soldier, "What have we done?" He replied, "Shut up. Your sin is that you are Muslim." Several hours later she saw her husband, he shook his head, signalling to her that it was not good. She overheard the soldiers asking, "What are we supposed to do with these men?" One told the other that they would wait for their commander to arrive and decide what would become of them. She heard later that the commander was of the 5th Battalion in the JNA. The soldiers dealt with the men by driving them away in green military vehicles. She never saw them again. The rest of the group was forced to stand out by the school on the road all day until nightfall. A bus arrived and they were then taken to the basement of a heating factory. There they had to sleep on concrete floors in the dark. There were bars on the windows. There were no toilets. They had to defecate on the floor. They stayed there for four days and four nights without food or water. The smallest children suffered the most. She convinced her son to urinate in a container, and because her breasts had dried up she fed her infant urine to prevent dehydration. She said a small Serb boy came to the window. She begged him to bring water for the children. She said he came back with a bottle of the water and poured it on the ground in front of them. In the middle of the night they heard heavy banging on the door like someone was trying to break it in. The women started screaming. Four or five men she identified as Chetniks entered the room with stockings over their heads and painted faces. "They were yelling, swearing, threatening to slaughter us and our children, calling us balijas." The room was dark. They tried to pick one woman, the one with the newborn. One of the Serbs said to leave her because she's no good to us, she just had a baby. They took other young women and her. She was interrogated. They asked her questions about what she knew. She said where she was from. She begged to be brought back to her children. Her interrogator said that information would come to her during the questioning. She knew nothing. Unspeakable acts followed. She was questioned about her marriage, her religion, whether she had any money, things that should not happen to women ever were inflicted on her. They put her back in the room with the other prisoners. She couldn't stop crying. The next day one of the men came and took her out again. She was afraid she was going to be executed. She asked to go back to her children. She never saw them again. Her ordeal continued; we will hear more about it during the trial. Eventually she was released and has spent the last 15 years searching for the bodies of her children, searching for the bodies of her husband. The destruction of her community, her life, her family exemplifies the product of the belligerent and bellicose nationalism propagated by the accused. The evidence will show that Mr. Seselj committed crimes during the Balkan wars. With the leading power structures in Serbia, he actively pursued the creation of an entity that he called Greater Serbia. Slobodan Milosevic shared this goal, but while Milosevic wouldn't dare call aloud for the liberation of Serb territory, Seselj would and did, and he repeatedly called for the "liberation" of what he said were Serb lands. Unfortunately, other people already lived there, people Seselj had no use for. The evidence will show that Milosevic first tried to keep Yugoslavia together. He tried to hold on to Croatia as Slovenia broke away, and when that failed he turned to separating the Krajina out of Croatia and then dividing up Bosnia and Herzegovina between Croatia and Serbia. Seselj joined him in this cause for Greater Serbia even though by definition it would require the taking by force of a large part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a large part of Croatia, and permanently expelling the non-Serb inhabitants. To achieve this goal, Milosevic and others sidelined moderate politicians and started wars throughout the Balkans. These wars destroyed cities, left hundreds of thousands displaced or dead, and attempted to wipe out entire groups based on their ethnicity, based on their religion, based on a perceived threat and hatred incited by the war propaganda of Mr. Seselj. The result of Seselj's pursuit of a Greater Serbia was the wholesale destruction of communities, the economic devastation and demoralization of the diverse peoples who made up the former Yugoslavia. The crimes were not simply against the communities within the former Yugoslavia, they were on a scale that concerns the international community. I pray the day of bellicose nationalism is over. In the end, Mr. Seselj did not achieve a Greater Serbia; he managed to achieve only a lesser Serbia and gave the world the phrase: Ethnic cleansing. How did this happen? We will follow the evidence to find the facts. Mr. Seselj is a master politician. The evidence will show that he is a shrewd and calculating man, a self-described scandal-monger. He calls himself the greatest living Serb nationalist, but he is wrong. National pride does not require fear and hatred and the destruction of cultures and religious that are different from one's own. The evidence will show, however, that this is the brand of nationalism that Mr. Seselj advocated during the period covered in the indictment between 1991 and 1993. He is not apologetic even today. His brand of nationalism is chauvinistic, belligerent, and poisonous to everyone. The evidence will show that Mr. Seselj, in a time of rapid change during the devolution of Yugoslavia, advocated violence against non-Serbs, and that during the conflict he adopted the role of a paramilitary commander and raised his own army of volunteers. The evidence will show that he indoctrinated them with his poisonous ideas and sent them to the front lines and to Muslim and Croat villages, where they and others committed unspeakable crimes. Some people say that there are so many wars in the Balkans that that's the nature of those people. It couldn't have been prevented, it's in their blood, it's in their genes; that is wrong. The Prosecution will present evidence that shows examples where countries in times of political change have chosen civic nationalism over ethnic nationalism, and that responsible political leadership promotes peace, reconciliation and the politics of inclusion. This did not have to happen, it was not inevitable. Mr. Seselj, however, presented himself during the conflict in this fashion, as a war-maker, armed with a rifle, and dressed in a traditional Serbian hat with a kokarda. His main tool for trying to achieve his goal of a Greater Serbia was his political party, the Serbian Radical Party. Through the political party, Mr. Seselj promoted a larger state for Serbs. He proclaimed the western borders should be along the line: Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica. Here you can see that the western borders go past even Bosnia and Herzegovina, through into Croatia, and that the Greater Serbia, and that the Greater Serbia pursued by Seselj included taking over the lands in other republics. Mr. Seselj organized the Radical Party and the Serbian Chetnik Movement within that through committees and a vast structure that included membership in many municipalities in other countries around the world as well, but he ruled it with an iron hand. He insisted to be kept informed of the most minute details and made all of the decisions. By nature the evidence will show that Mr. Seselj is an autocrat. Witnesses will tell you that when talking with his associates, whether from the Radical Party or the Chetnik Movement, Mr. Seselj would always do so in a raised voice, making it clear that he was in charge and that what he proposed had to be done. The Serbian Chetnik Movement was a part the Radical Party, a movement that according to the statute of the Radical Party would be the military wing during conflict. He organized the volunteers into a command structure and the volunteers considered them to be his leader [sic]. He describes himself as the only Serbian Chetnik Vojvoda, or duke, directly engaged in the ongoing liberation movement of the Serbian people, following in the tradition of Serbian Chetniks. The Prosecution will prove that together with others, Seselj implemented the common objective of permanently expelling non-Serbs from territories that Seselj claimed to belong to Serbs. He promoted the expulsion of non-Serbs from specific targeted territory. He incited his audience to expel Serbs [sic], and he recruited and indoctrinated volunteers to serve in the war effort, to serve in the military and pursue this goal with brutal force. His fanatical and extreme rhetoric attracted many young men who volunteered to serve in his cause. They became part of the thousands of volunteers who fought on the front lines in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. The evidence will show that the professional army considered them thugs. They quickly earned a reputation for being undisciplined and violent and criminal; however, they served a purpose. Seselj's volunteers did what no one would say out loud was necessary. Seselj's extreme rhetoric not only attracted men and women who volunteered for the war, but it also influenced other soldiers and volunteers and militias who fought in both the army and Territorial Defences and instilled in these Serbs fear and hatred of Croats and Muslims and the desire to create a homeland for Serbs, a Greater Serbia. We will also hear how Seselj's extreme rhetoric had a strong and immediate effect on Croats and Muslims. Just hearing Seselj's fiery speeches and his terrifying threats was enough to make people flee for their lives. They left their homes and tried to get to safety. Mr. Seselj has claimed in these proceedings that he has been charged with a new crime, an invented crime. Unfortunately, war propaganda and hate speech is not new at all. The evidence will show that Seselj used tried-and-true propaganda techniques to poison the minds of his listeners in order to further his criminal goals. Before the 1990s, ethnic relations between neighbours were stable. The past was the past. The mindset of ordinary civilians was one of normal life. Yugoslavia is a mosaic of diverse peoples with neighbourhoods mixed. Bosnia and Herzegovina had a proud tradition of intermarriage and peaceful living. Seselj called upon the wounds of the past to incite a crisis mentality. As the bonds holding the republic began to dissolve and as communism loosened its grip on the former Yugoslavia, people like Milosevic and the Croatian President Franjo Tudjman and Mr. Seselj knew that extreme nationalism could become a political force that would keep them or bring them to power. This war was fought first with words. I want to show you a video from April 1991 with Mr. Seselj in an atmosphere that describes very closely the amount of public support and energy that he created when he advocated for a Serbian homeland.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "In such an atmosphere Vojvoda Seselj, announced already at the beginning of the meeting, started his speech. "Voja! Voja! Serbia! Serbia! Serbia! Serbia! Serbia! Serbia! "This is where Serbian people live, this is Serbian land and it will remain Serbian forever. "Audience: That's right. "Journalist: Instead of calming them down, special sent a message to the people at the end: "Brothers and sisters, we are sending a message to the new Ustasha regime. It is the most difficult for you. He promised them that they would not remain on their own and that all Serbs had just one party and that is the Serb Radical Party. You have the hero Milan Babic at your helm. He called those who separate the Serbian people traitors. Ante Markovic and other foreign services consider today that there are more important problems than your defence and your protection. They are offering you to Tudjman. They want to hand you over. You will not be handed over. "Instead of calming them down, Seselj sent a message to the gathered people at the end: "We are sending a message to the new Ustasha head of state and Ustasha regime in Croatia: Serbian heads have rolled, struck down by the Ustasha hand in Serbian Krajina. A Serbian head has rolled in Serbian Western Srem and Slavonia as well. We will avenge Serbian blood. "Audience: We will. "When it seemed after Seselj's speech that there would be no response to his call to attack Plitvice, there was a blockade. In spite of what the JNA officer said ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj's prophecy of heads to roll would prove true. His brand of bellicose nationalism and persistent threat of public advocation of threats and violence primed people to accept what was necessary to achieve his goals. Without Seselj's ability and determination to instill his vision of reality into the minds of fellow Serbs, there would have been few tools, no armed men to carry out the violent goals of the Serb political and military leadership to create a Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "As far as we are concerned, the Croats can leave Yugoslavia any time they want, but we are letting them know openly that they will not take a single inch of Serbian territory, not a piece of land on which there are Serb villages, demolished churches, pits in which Serbs were butchered, Serbian camps, Serbian killing fields, such as a Jasenovac. Should we permit that, we would be unworthy of our glorious ancestors and shamed before our descendants. The Croats may create their new state but only to the west of the Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica line. Everything to the east of that line is Serbian. We shall not allow the Croats to manipulate the Bunjevci Serbs and the Sokci Serbs. They are Catholic Serbs who, we hope, will soon realise what kind of role the Vatican and the Ustasha leadership has in store for them against the Serbian people."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In this one speech we can take note of several propaganda techniques, expert testimony will help to frame Mr. Seselj's political discourse. He sent out threat messages, that people were threatened. He traded on wounds of the past. He glorified his own group, and he denigrated those outside his group. Seselj's alliance and working in concert with Mr. Milosevic gave him the ability to broadcast his propaganda in the public media and to exert his influence in the arenas of both politics and military power at the same time. He was able to recruit and indoctrinate people willing to wage war to establish his Greater Serbia. He was prolific in his speeches.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica has to be our goal, and that is the border where the army has to withdraw all its troops. If the army is unable to move its troops from Zagreb to this line without a fight, then they should do this with force and with the bombing of Zagreb. The army still has capacities which it has not yet used. If its troops are endangered, it has the right to use napalm bombs and anything else they have available in their warehouses. We cannot play games here. It is more important to save one army unit than to worry if there will be some accidental victims. Who's to blame here? They wanted war, now they have it."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: By mid-1991 Mr. Seselj had refined his rhetorical skills and had convinced others that members of other ethnic groups, particularly Croats, posed a grave danger to the survival of the Serbs as a group. He called Croats Ustashas, linking them to the fascist regime that collaborated with Nazi Germany during World War II. He constantly reminded Serb populations that they were victims of the past and of present crimes committed by Croats and others. He skilfully used that sense of victimhood as justification for acts of collective violence and revenge.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The new Ustasha chief and Josip Broz General Franjo Tudjman and the new Ustasha government in Croatia have again put the criminal Kama under the throat of the Serbian people. Should they attempt a new genocide against the Serbian people, we will not allow them to happen again. We say to them we shall take revenge for each Serbian life and we shall also ask to pay up for past crimes. Also for crimes in recent history. Nothing will remain unpunished and we will not allow the consequences of the occupation of the Serb lands and the Serb people."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Seselj's speeches demonized and dehumanized Croats, Muslims, and other groups by portraying them using negative stereotypes, in addition to linking all Croats to the fascist Ustasha regime, he labelled Bosniaks as supporters of a pan-Islamic movement that allegedly intended to take control of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He publishes his speeches and his interviews and in an interview that he has reprinted in a book called: "Politics as a conscientious challenge," under the title: "Chetnik revenge will be blind," we see an example of this stereotyping from May 1991. "How is one supposed to negotiate with the Ustashas? Do you see today that the Croatian people with entirely Ustasha? There are very few exceptions." By using these dehumanizing stereotypes, Seselj removed the need to question the morality or legality of crimes committed against Croats and Muslims, at the same time his speeches glorified the Serb people and their behaviour in wartime, which further encouraged aggression and violence against other groups. As an example of Serb glorification, I began turn to another book published by Mr. Seselj entitled: "Serbian Chetnik Movement." From there we see a newspaper reprint where he is greeting the heroic leader of Milan Babic, "who is in the front lines of the defence of Serb-dom, whose intelligence and courage placed him among the greatest sons of Serbian people, and we would tell him that thousands of Chetniks will jump to his aid every time he seeks help. We also greet the SDS of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its clever leader Dr. Karadzic, who stood in the front lines in the defence of national interests through the will of the Serbian people. We would tell them all that they -- we will tell them all that they will not stand alone as long as Serbian Chetniks are ready to follow the glorious examples of their forebears." Mr. Seselj gave countless speeches, continuing the process of continuing large segments of the Serb population that they were endangered, that Croats and Muslims were to be feared and hated, and that action, including extreme and violent action, had to be taken quickly to protect against the grave threat facing Serbs. The language that Seselj used made his speech criminal. In the context of a volatile war and political turmoil where people already susceptible to messages of fear and hate, Seselj was also fully aware of his own political power and his extraordinary ability to influence people by his words. He was interviewed for a documentary which is now well-known and he made statements during his testimony in the trial of Slobodan Milosevic. These illustrate the power of his rhetoric.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Milan Babic came with me and the people sort of booed him, but then I gave a fiery speech and then people started applauding Babic. Milan Babic wanted to reconcile with Raskovic, but Raskovic refused on the spot and that's why he failed."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I first went there on the 9th of March when Vuk Draskovic was tearing Belgrade down. I went to Slavonia to start an uprising of the Serbian people. I am proud of the role I played in 1991. The Serbs there asked for me, they called me. First of all, they did not trust Milosevic much. He gave them some promises, but he did not always keep them. They felt threatened, and because we at the Serbian Chetnik Movement gathered a large number of decisive, capable, and courageous people, they asked for our help."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: During Mr. Milosevic's appearance at the Milosevic trial Judge Bonomy asked him: "How many volunteers were there from the Radical Party?" Mr. Seselj answered saying: "Well, sort of for propaganda reasons we said that there were about 30.000 of them, but the real figure would have been about 10.000." That was enough. The Prosecution's evidence will prove that when Mr. Seselj used political speech to generate fear and hatred, his actions were calculated and deliberate. His hate speech harmed the human dignity of communities that he targeted. And the Prosecution will lead evidence that will support a finding that he persecuted people with his speech. Concerning the charges in the indictment, we'll show you evidence that Mr. Seselj's speeches directly instigated and incited Serb men and women to commit acts of violence against Muslims and Croats in Vukovar in 1991, in Zvornik in the spring of 1992, and Hrtkovci in the spring and summer of 1992. Seselj's speeches also made a significant contribution to the work of high-level political and military leaders engaged in the criminal enterprise to forcibly remove large numbers of non-Serbs from their homes. We will also present evidence that his speeches caused people to flee, satisfying the elements of the crimes against humanity of deportation and forcible transfer. Seselj's criminal forms of public expression were highly effective in the province of Vojvodina, Serbia, which was home to more than 72.000 ethnic Croats before the war started. Vojvodina is the province of Serbia which borders Croatia, namely Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. Many volunteers for the Radical Party and the Chetnik Movement were recruited from Vojvodina, and Seselj visited different locations in Vojvodina on numerous occasions. You will hear from the Prosecution's expert demographer Ewa Tabeau, that during 1991 and 1992 close to 250.000 ethnic Serb refugees came to Serbia from Croatia and parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. More than 95.000 of these ethnic refugees arrived in Vojvodina, some of them on buses arranged by the Radical Party. To make room for these refugees and to further his own political agenda, Seselj spoke at rallies, at private meetings, and in the Serbian parliament, calling for the expulsion of Croats from Vojvodina. He declared Croats in Serbia to be disloyal citizens who had to be expelled. Next I will show you a speech from parliament.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Believing that the argument was not moving in the right direction, Seselj asked to speak again. The briefest gist of his discussion this time could be described as a suggestion that if the Croats were expelling the Serbs from Zagreb, what were the Croats waiting for in Belgrade? Mahmud Mehic and Ahmet Skenderovic responded to this saying ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Seselj reprinted his speech before the Assembly in Serbia in April 1992. He said: "Another issue: If the Croats are chasing the Serbs away from their homes like this on a large scale, what are the Croats here in Belgrade waiting for, what are the Croats all over Serbia waiting for? An exchange of population: We chase away as many Croats from Belgrade as there are Serbs whom Tudjman has chased away from Zagreb. When a Serbian family arrives from Zagreb, well, they should simply go to the address of a Croat in Belgrade and give them their keys, go away to Zagreb, an exchange ... The Croats in Slankamen and Zemun and in other locations will not sleep in peace until they move out ... We will not kill you, that goes without saying, but what we will do is simply pack you up in trucks and trains and you just go off and get along in Zagreb." In fact, they did kill the Croats, and they were packed up and sent away. Ethnic Croats living in the farming village of Hrtkovci, about an hour's drive north-west of Belgrade, were some of the victims of Mr. Seselj's campaign to drive Croats out of Serbia. Tensions began to rise in Hrtkovci during the second half of 1991 with the arrival of refugees. On the 6th of May -- I'm sorry. Serbs from outside Hrtkovci, as well as Serb residents of the village associated with the SRS harassed and threatened prominent Croat residents and told them to leave the village. Seselj appeared at a public rally in Hrtkovci on 6 May 1992 that had been organized by the SRS. Prosecution witnesses will describe how Seselj called for the expulsion of the Croats from that community. Mr. Seselj is proud of his speech and has reprinted it in yet another book. His speech is entitled: "The vital importance of May elections - Promotion Rally of the Serbian Radical Party, Hrtkovci." He's published it in a book called: "The Devil's Apprentice - Criminal Roman Pope John Paul II." Here's what he told the people: "In this village, too, in Hrtkovci, in this place in Serbian Srem, there is no room for Croats. Who are those Croats for whom there is room among us? Only those Croats and their families who have shed blood together with us on the front lines. They were called Croats in name only, anyway. Some of them served with our volunteers. They have already awakened to the fact that they are, in fact, Catholic Serbs. They will stay here with us while all the rest must clear out of Serbia, including those from here, from Hrtkovci, who locked up their houses and left, reckoning, I suppose, that they would come back one day, but our message to them is: No, you have nowhere to return to. Serbian refugees will move into their houses. "Serbian brothers and sisters, now that Tudjman has expelled more than 200.000 Serbs, a part of them will return to the area of Serbian Krajina, but another part cannot find a place for them here. We have to give those Serbs a roof over their heads and feed the hungry mouths. We have no money to build new housing. We do not have the capacity to create new jobs for them. Very well then, if we cannot do that, then we should give every Serbian family of refugees the address of one Croatian family. The police will give it to them, the police will do as the government decides, and we will be the government soon. Fine, then. Every Serbian family of refugees will knock on one Croatian door and give whatever Croats they find their address in Zagreb or another Croatian place. Oh, they will, they will. There will be enough buses. We will drive them to the border of Serbian territory and they can walk on from there, if they do not leave before of their own accord." I'll skip down. "I firmly believe that you, Serbs from Hrtkovci and other villages around here will know how to preserve your harmony and unify and that you will promptly get rid of the remaining Croats in our village and in the surrounding villages ..." Prosecution witnesses will describe the fear, the terror caused by Seselj's appearance and speech in their community, and they will explain why they decided to abandon their homes as a result. Their fears were justified. Witnesses will describe the vicious campaign that Seselj's speech unleashed to expel the ethnic Croat residents of Hrtkovci. The expulsion campaign mirrored the instructions in Seselj's speech: Croat residents were harassed and intimidated. They received telephone threats, they were beaten, hand-grenades thrown on to their property, they were coerced to exchange their houses, and their houses were outright confiscated. Seselj later talked about the events in Hrtkovci and in Vojvodina overall. The words he chose provide examples of another common tool of propaganda: They use lies when it suits them. We will present evidence that after the expulsion of Croats from Hrtkovci and Vojvodina, Seselj described this as a voluntary exchange of properties between Croats and Serbs. He sanitized the violence and lied by calling it voluntary. The Prosecution will present evidence that in response to questions and criticism about the expulsions of non-Serbs from Hrtkovci and other communities in Vojvodina, Seselj had this to say for himself, again this is drawn from another one of his books. In a radio programme in December 1993, Mr. Seselj said: "We stood for a civilised exchange of population with Croatia. If you remember, we insisted on that two years ago. Those were our efforts, mostly our efforts that enabled this exchange to take place. The clotures from Hrtkovci moved to Croatia, and the Serbs that Tudjman previously expelled from Croatia came to Hrtkovci. This happened in Kukujevci, Petrovaradin, Slankamen, Beska and partially in many other places. You know, we are the opposition party and it seems to me that we accomplished the maximum in this field. In this exchange of properties, the Croats were given a lot more in Croatia than the Serbs received here from what the Croats left for them in exchange." Dr. Seselj said: "It was supposed to be conducted in a more civilised way than it was actually carried out, but in any case we are satisfied with the results. Thousands of Serbian families were accommodated in some extent, they were given houses and apartments in Hrtkovci ... And the Croats were not damaged at all, they were given even more. They went to their country and they received better houses than the ones they left." This became known as ethnic cleansing in other parts of the former Yugoslavia. Mr. Seselj's discourse transforms it into a civilised exchange of population. The Prosecution evidence will show that these lies served an important purpose, they allowed people to avoid the inconvenient and moral and legal questions about their behaviour toward others. These distortions of history provided Serbs with a simpler moral framework that permitted them to accept and commit acts of violence against their neighbours. Seselj performed a crucial act in furtherance of the pursuit of Greater Serbia, his use of hate speech primed people to condone the collective violence. At this point I would like to ask whether it would be appropriate to have a short break to allow the interpreters and the court reporters. We've been going for over an hour and I want to ensure accuracy in the translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you are asking for a break, that's not a problem. We will have a 20-minute break and resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have resumed our hearing. Mrs. Dahl, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll return briefly to Mr. Seselj's speeches and use of the media and then turn to what happened on the ground. Mr. Seselj, as our evidence will show, used all available media resources to send his message. He appeared on television, he appeared on radio, daily newspapers, including two newspapers published by his own political party, one printed in Belgrade and the other in Banja Luka, disseminated his ideology. Weekly periodicals carried his message and he made an enormous number of personal appearances to disseminate his hate speech. In July 1993 the issue of Western Serbia, one of the Radical Party's newspapers, carried this offensive cartoon. The cartoon depicts a large Serbian Orthodox church and a man with a broom sweeping away small pieces of a mosque from the area around the church. The article -- the cartoon appeared with an article entitled: "There is no co-existence with Islam." By the time this article appeared with this cartoon, the message it promoted had been largely fulfilled. Serbs had destroyed Muslim cultural property as a means of destroying the Muslim identity and presence in communities throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina. Seselj republished his speeches and interviews and articles in scores of books, which continue to be published, advertised, sold, read, and reviewed in the Balkans. We will bring to you excerpts and analysis of 66 volumes of Mr. Seselj's published works. This case calls upon us to ask how can this happen? How does collective violence appear? How do neighbour turn against neighbour? It is in the basics of human nature that we find the answer. We will present evidence that explains how every person is susceptible to the conditioning of fear-based rhetoric and how in crisis conditions, as developed in the former Yugoslavia, bring people one short step from an ordinary living in community to the fearful and violent destruction of a community. History teaches us over and over again the banality of evil and how ordinary people, in circumstances we hope never to imagine, can commit the most terrible acts, from Nazi Germany to Cambodia to the former Yugoslavia to Rwanda, these terrible acts are not the misguided deeds of a few psychopaths, but rather they result from political and military leadership instead of teaching peace and civic nationalism, teaching instead a brutal and bellicose ideology, providing the public with a steady stream of propaganda that promotes and justifies that ideology, and organizes the population at large to accept a smaller group of violent perpetrators engaging in violent acts to exterminate their neighbours. The news coverage in the region captured volunteers, explaining why they were going to war.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Will be Serbian, ours. It won't belong to the Ustashas anymore. There will be no more fascism. It's enough. We have suffered it for 50 years. We were waiting. They hate us. It's enough. It's the end now. "We have to fight with them. "Why? "Because: [In English] The head of the kid is on the pig and the head of the pig is on the kid's body. Do you know what that means? Do you see that? Them people discuss, never, only fight to the end, the last, the last boot, the last Ustasha. "Hey, let’s go to the company."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: That clip was from militias in Vukovar. Beyond mere words, Mr. Seselj also contributed his actions. He and his associates helped finance, supply, and direct the actions of the volunteers who joined up with other Serb forces to "liberate" Serb territories and expel their populations. We will present evidence showing that even though these volunteers were subordinated to military commanders in the field, they often stayed together in units and detachments who were commanded by squad leaders from the SRS. We will bring you evidence that these leaders reported back to both the front line commanders and to Seselj and his associates in the party offices back in Belgrade. Seselj and his associates didn't just stay in Belgrade, however. They helped to plan and prepare take-overs in strategic locations in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now I will talk in some more detail about the military structure of the armed forces involved in the war. Yugoslavia's founder, Tito, established a two-tier military structure. This included both the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA, and a sustainable all people's army, called the Territorial Defence. The Territorial Defence was designed to protect against standing military being crushed by the numerically superior Soviet forces. We will present evidence that the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA, constituted the national armed force; it was an active-duty, conventional military under centralised control from Belgrade. It possessed all the armour, mechanised fighting vehicles, and heavy artillery. Its mission was to challenge any invasion and delay the enemy long enough for the Territorial Defence to mobilise. Conversely, the Territorial Defence had a decentralised command structure that could not be wiped out in a single blow. It was essentially under the command of each republic's political authorities, and the Territorial Defence system relied upon country-wide military training for the entire male population and massive stockpiles of small arms, caches of light weapons such as mortars and vast quantities of ammunition. The military mission of the Territorial Defence was to mount a protracted partisan-type war against any invasion force, even if much of the country was occupied. The real object was to deter invasion in the first place by making it potentially so costly that an enemy would not pursue it. The Territorial Defences developed into semi-autonomous military forces answering to the republics. By the end of the 1980s, they could be perceived as threats to the Yugoslav Army and its centralised command coming out of Belgrade. To understand the conflict, we must look at the transformation of the army as the political bonds holding the former Yugoslavia dissolved. The socialist Presidency was the most senior command and control of the socialist armed forces. If there were declared a state of emergency or a state of war or an imminent threat of war, the socialist Presidency would become the Supreme Command, assisted by a command staff. The indictment names as members of the joint criminal enterprise General Veljko Kadijevic, who served as Minister of Defence and general of the army between 1988 and 1992, and Colonel-General Blagoje Adzic. He succeeded General Kadijevic in 1992 and served as Federal Secretary of the People's Defence. Before the conflict, the law in Yugoslavia allowed for people who were not already conscripts to join up or volunteer for military service with either the JNA or the Territorial Defence. The law did not, however, authorise the formation of volunteer units by nationalist political parties or other groups outside the framework of the Yugoslavian armed forces, either in the JNA or in the Territorial Defences. Apart from the state, no one else was authorised by law to organize, reinforce, arm, equip, or train armed forces. Nevertheless, the JNA knew that Seselj's volunteers were operating in Croatia. During the conflict in Croatia, nationalist political parties in Serbia, like Seselj's Radical Party, organized the recruitment, training, and dispatching of volunteers to conflict zones; they even set up their own volunteer or paramilitary formations. The evidence will show that this was with the tacit authorisation of the Government of the Republic of Serbia. The volunteers affiliated with Seselj's Radical Party or the Chetnik Movement used the name of Chetnik or Seselj's Men to describe themselves. At the same time, there were also other groups such as Arkan's Tigers, commanded by Zeljko Raznatovic, who went by his nickname Arkan, and volunteers operating under the command of Dragan Vasiljkovic, also known as Captain Dragan, which according to the evidence we will bring you, intelligence reports prepared by the JNA security organs, security administration, these groups maintained close ties with the Ministry of the Interior and the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbia. The indictment identifies as members of the joint criminal enterprise the leaders of these state organs: The head of the state security in Serbia, Jovica Stanisic; and the head of the Serbian secret police, the Ministry of Internal Affairs, Franko Simatovic; under them was Radovan Stojcic, also known as Badza, an official of Serbian Ministry of the Interior, in charge of operations in Eastern Slavonia. The Supreme Command of the JNA and Serbian authorities were aware that volunteers were participating in the conflict in Croatia and they were aware of and encouraged the role of national political parties in the recruitment of these volunteers. After Slovenia and Croatia declared independence, the mission of the Yugoslav armed forces began to change. The JNA began to suffer desertion, its soldiers were unwilling to fight in a civil war. As the JNA withdrew from Slovenia, it slowly transformed away from being a Yugoslav Army into being a Serb army. We will present evidence showing that its mission changed from safe-guarding territorial integrity into consolidating Serb control of targeted areas in order to protect the Serb population. Seselj explicitly approved the shift of the role of the JNA in Croatia, and he underlined the complementarity of the JNA and the Seselj volunteers in implementing what he perceived as common goals. We will present evidence that during the spring of 1991 Seselj made several calls for the unification of all lands he considered Serb along the Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica line. Later on in the conflict when he realised that Serb forces had not achieved that line, that they had not claimed the western border of Serb lands, he blamed the federal secretary for the people's defence, army General Kadijevic for this failure. The Radical Party's founding statute or its party statute identifies its goal as the struggle for the unification of all Serbian lands into one state and the protection of Serbs in territories belonging to other states. Even though in his numerous public appearances, Seselj emphasised that his role and the role of the party in relation to volunteers was limited to the gathering and dispatching of these volunteers, documents produced by the Radical Party itself, including articles that were published in Seselj's party magazine "Velika Srbija," demonstrate that Seselj's role and the role of his volunteers in the war was much wider. We will present evidence showing that the Radical Party's war staff maintained close relations with the Radical Party volunteers, even after they were sent to be commanded by either the JNA or the local Territorial Defence units. The close relations maintained by the Radical Party war staff included issuing orders, giving instructions, exchanging operational information, keeping records of deployed volunteers and their performance, and the performance of fact-finding missions by senior members of the Radical Party war staff. Seselj's public statements indicate that he knew what his volunteers were doing when they were engaged in combat activities. We can see from Mr. Seselj's later promotion of his volunteer leaders that he approved of what they did. We will bring you evidence that shows in 1993 and 1994 he promoted men who, according to him, had distinguished themselves in the armed conflict in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. He promoted them and gave them the title of Vojvoda. A Chetnik Vojvoda, according to the Radical Party documentation, attaches to the most senior commanding officers within their military volunteer hierarchy. Seselj's volunteers drew first blood in Croatia. We will present evidence that on May 2nd, 1991, a group of Seselj's volunteers ambushed policemen, Croatian policemen, in Borovo Selo in their first armed action. These volunteers who, according to Seselj "proved competent during the defence of Borovo Selo" were promoted to the title of Vojvoda on 12 May of 1991. The coordination by the relevant military and political structures is demonstrated by the Radical Party's establishment of first a Crisis Staff in April 1991 and then it transformation on 1 October 1991 into a War Staff. We will demonstrate that the War Staff played a key role in the recruitment and dispatching of volunteers. In order to achieve this task, the War Staff cooperated with the Ministry of the Interior, the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbia, and with the JNA. We will present evidence that volunteers recruited by Seselj or Seselj's party were trained and equipped, including the provision of weapons and ammunitions at the JNA or the Ministry of the Interior facilities or with other assistance of the existing military structures. The Radical Party War Staff also organized the payment of volunteers or their relatives in coordination with other government arms, such as the Serbian Ministry for Relations with Serbs outside Serbia. I want to turn now to Croatia and the battle for Vukovar. The Prosecution will present evidence that before the outbreak of the conflict in Croatia, the police and the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Croatia gradually split into Croatian and local Serb structures. In areas where Serbs had a majority or a significant minority, they took over the existing structures, as the non-Serbs had left or were encouraged to leave, or did not recognise the Socialist Federal Republic anymore and ceased their cooperation with the JNA, or local Serbs set up their own police and Territorial Defence units and staffed these units with people who did not answer to the republican authorities in Croatia, but stayed loyal to what remained of the Socialist Federal Republic, and Serbia. During combat operations in Croatia, the JNA established operational and tactical groups to restore and maintain unified and single command and control between the JNA, local Serb Territorial Defence, local Serb police, and the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Serbia as well as the units and detachments of volunteers. In September 1991, the JNA endeavoured to keep Vukovar part of the Federation instead of allowing Croatia to secede. The operational groups that covered Vukovar consisted of JNA units, local Territorial Defence, and Serbian volunteers, including those affiliated with or sent by the Radical Party and Arkan's Tigers. Arkan's Tigers mainly participated in the operational areas of the north, Seselj's volunteers were predominantly active in two detachments in Vukovar known as Petrova Gora and Leva Supoderica. The Radical Party War Staff maintained close relationships with the local Vukovar territorial command. It was led by a man named Kameni, and he was considered a Chetnik detachment commander. We will hear evidence that on 9th November of 1991, the chief of the SRS War Staff instructed the commander of that detachment to appoint subordinate commanders and to put all volunteers under their command. Seselj visited his volunteers in Vukovar. Strict orders from the JNA attempted to maintain control over the volunteers. The Chetnik commander of Vukovar on December 9, 1991, requested promotions for his warriors. He asked the chief of the War Staff, and he mentioned the commanders in Vukovar. By then the massacres at Ovcara and Velepromet had happened. Seselj promoted Kameni and others in 1993 and 1994 for their service at Vukovar. The human rights abuses taking place in Vukovar were well-known worldwide. For example, on January 21, 1992, Helsinki Watch sent a letter alerting Slobodan Milosevic to human rights abuses. The report attached to the letter explicitly mentioned the summary execution of people evacuated from the hospital at Vukovar at Ovcara on the evening of 20/21 November 1991. We will present evidence that on 18 November 1991 when Vukovar fell to the Serb forces, an elderly man and his wife, fearing the worst, went to the hospital to find protection. The following day Serb forces took away non-Serbs. They threatened them and cursed them and eventually they arrived at Ovcara farm. There they were beaten by soldiers and subjected to all manner of cruelty. Some were killed right there and then in the hangar or in front of the hangar. The elderly man who will testify here survived because he knew one of the soldiers. That soldier saved his life. The other men and a few women who were massacred were buried in a mass grave. The Prosecution will show that Seselj decided that the Radical Party should send as many as his volunteers as possible to Vukovar. We will bring you documentation, as described, that shows the chain of command, the delivery of volunteers, the presence of their detachment, and the role that they play. We will provide testimony of soldiers regarding the coordination of Kameni with the commanders of the Territorial Defence and the Yugoslav Army brigades in Vukovar. Seselj himself said on TV on the 23rd of November, 1991, that "Kameni, our main commander in Vukovar plans his action with the army major in the evening and executes it the next day. The army did not have enough manpower to go around capturing each house because of desertion. That is what our men did." A few days before the massacre at Ovcara Seselj went to Vukovar to visit his volunteers and boost their morale. The Prosecution will present evidence that he participated in a meeting with the commanders of the Territorial Defence and the JNA and Seselj said: "We are all one army. This war is a great test for Serbs. Those who pass the test will become winners. Deserters cannot go unpunished. Not a single Ustasha must leave Vukovar alive." The soldiers did what Seselj requested them to do. When Serb forces occupied the city, hundreds of Croats were killed by Serbs. Among those committing the murders at Ovcara and elsewhere in Vukovar were the Seselj volunteers, commanded by Kameni. This photo is of Mr. Seselj in the ruins of Vukovar, to his left is Kameni. We will hear from witnesses present at the Vukovar Hospital, at the Vukovar barracks, and Ovcara that the Seselj volunteers led by Kameni wanted revenge on those who had been taken from the Vukovar Hospital. The evidence will show that many Seselj volunteers participated in the mass murders at Ovcara. We will hear from witnesses that the man Kameni was -- that Kameni was close to Seselj. He had direct access to him and reported to him personally. Recently, Kameni was convicted and sentenced to 20 years' imprisonment in Belgrade for his participation in the atrocities committed at Ovcara. This photograph shows Kameni with several other Vojvodas in 1993. Seselj promoted Kameni to the rank of Vojvoda in 1993 for their achievements during the Vukovar campaign and elsewhere. He promoted a man named Vakic who participated in the ambush on the policemen at Borovo Selo. He also recognised his other participation in Chetnik units he described as operating in Serbian Herzegovina in May and June of 1992. In this same promotion order Seselj recognises Milan Lancuzanin as the best of the best and as an excellent commander of the Leva Supoderica volunteer unit of the Radical Party at Vukovar. What the order promoting these men fails to mention but what the evidence will show is that wherever these two men were active, non-Serbs were murdered. These two were not the only perpetrators of crimes against humanity who were promoted by Seselj. Topola, another Chetnik volunteer who was present at Ovcara, killed Croats elsewhere in Vukovar, including at the Velepromet facility close to the JNA barracks used by the Serb forces as a detention facility for Croats and others. After the fall of Vukovar, Topola and some other volunteers removed detainees from the room and killed them. The evidence will show that when Seselj was informed about the crimes Topola committed, he simply said: "What can I do now? Disarm the man and send him home, he's tired." Seselj and his associates did not report these crimes to Serbian authorities; instead, they deployed him as a volunteer to Bosnia and Herzegovina, where he repeated his prior acts and committed more serious crimes against the non-Serb population. After Vukovar came Vocin. December 1991, you can see looking at the western-most line of cities that if Seselj wanted to create a homogenous Greater Serbia they would need to take Vocin. That was a town that had a Croatian population of approximately 1500 people. When Serb forces were in control of Vocin, they massacred the population; upon their withdrawal, people went into Vocin and found civilians who had been murdered by a blow of an axe to their face, by gun-shot wounds into their eyes, by bullets to the back. We will provide evidence to show that this campaign, this devastation of Vocin, the destruction of the Catholic church there was designed to terrorise and cause, and in fact caused, the flight of the civilian populations. Seselj transferred his volunteers to Vocin where they terrorised the non-Serb population and persecuted them based on their ethnicity. We will provide evidence on the extensive cooperation between the Territorial Defence in Western Slavonia and the SRS headquarters in Belgrade. This includes requests for volunteers originating from the region and the approval and dispatch of those volunteers by the Radical Party. SRS headquarters, the evidence will show, worked hand and glove with both the JNA and local authorities throughout the conflict in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Let me refer again to the basic military organization that Seselj maintained for the Radical Party volunteers. His volunteers had specific commanders from the party ranks. Rule 7 from the basic military organization says that: "The volunteer units of the Serbian Radical Party are engaged in combat or other combat-related activities independently or as part of the appropriate unit of the Yugoslav Army, the Army of Republika Srpska, or Army of Serbian Krajina, according to the plans made by the commands of the aforementioned armies. "Volunteer units are engaged in these armies only in their entirety and under the command of the volunteer commanders, exceptions possible if arranged." In this connection, a volunteer commander in full authority and responsibility, is delegated to the specific command to coordinate possibilities, requests, requirements, utilisation, and security of the volunteer units. The rules of the Radical Party also made reference to the hierarchical command structure. It says: "The commands of the Serbian Radical Party volunteers are organized as commanding organs for all volunteer forces, their units, and their combat activities. They are formed analogously to the commanding structure of the party organs." Witnesses will tell us that at times the Radical Party transferred volunteers of its party and other volunteers from elsewhere to the front lines together. For the local population, the volunteers were just the same. Their presence created a climate of fear. They looted, they threatened, they abused, and they killed. What is important is that the evidence will show that these volunteers considered themselves Chetniks and approved of, followed, pursued, executed Seselj's goal of creating a Greater Serbia. Let me read to you what one of the volunteers said when referring to a gathering of the Serbian Chetnik Movement in Ravna Gora in May 1990. I quote: "All the parties were present more or less the same. Vojislav Seselj, Mirko Jovic, and Vuk Draskovic held speeches during the rally. The things that were said during the speeches were almost all the same ..." This witness sometime later joined the SRS because he thought: "Draskovic," and I'm devoting his words, "was too moderate, and Seselj with his more radical stance impressed me more." In November 1991, Seselj visited Vocin and met his volunteers. We will hear from local witnesses that after the volunteers had a meeting with Seselj, they became more aggressive and there was a sharp increase in crimes against Croat civilians. The criminal conduct of the volunteers was known to human rights observers as well as the armies that took control later in Bosnia. For example, in a report prepared in July of 1992 entitled: "Report on paramilitary formations in the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina" by the Main Staff of the VRS, they say this of the volunteers: "They are mainly composed of individuals of low moral quality, and in many cases of persons previously prosecuted for crimes and offences and even convicted of murder, robbery, and larceny and the light. Very often, such units have in their ranks pathological criminals whom the conditions of war and general lawlessness have brought to the fore ..." I continue their report: "Many formations of this type display hatred of non-Serbian peoples and one can conclude without reservations that they are the genocidal elements among the Serbian people ... War profiteering and looting are the motive for the great majority of paramilitaries ... One common feature to all paramilitary formations is that they do not take part in direct fighting with the enemy. Instead, they are operating behind the lines of the regular Serbian Republic Bosnia and Herzegovina army units, and looting and burning property and killing the innocent population." This report identifies by name many of the units they're describing. They mention Seselj's men, Seseljevci, a term used by the volunteers. The Prosecution will provide evidence that he was fully apprised of the types of people who had joined the ranks of the Radical Party volunteers and the other volunteers he assisted in transferring to the regions in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Both Radical Party members and local officials told Seselj and his associates in the SRS office in Belgrade about the unruly and cruel behaviour of the volunteers on the ground. That information was met with indifference and hostility. Seselj's associates kept him informed, and he also made very many visits to the front lines. With his own eyes he saw the destruction being wrought by the Serb forces on Muslim and Croat villages and communities. As a leading politician and a member of the Serbian parliament, Seselj of course had many ways to receive information. A large amount of information was available in the public domain as well. Surely he will not claim ignorance. We will prove that he knew what was happening and he persisted in his aims, knowing the crimes of mass scales were being committed. I want to turn now to Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Serbs pursued war aims in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992. They wanted to create a territorially contiguous Bosnian Serb state. They made extensive pre-war preparations for the secession from Bosnia. As Croatia and Slovenia were trying to secede from the republic, so too was Bosnia and Herzegovina. But within that, the Bosnian Serbs were trying to secede themselves and remain attached to the Serbian majority populations in the neighbouring republics. We will present evidence that the JNA backed the Serbs in early 1992 and transformed JNA units into a Bosnian Serb army, that was an incredibly important factor in their ability to fight and gain territorial control. During the winter of 1991, what remained of the political leadership of Yugoslavia discussed the future of the army in Bosnia and Herzegovina in light of the recognition of Slovenia and Croatia. High-level political and military leaders, we will present evidence to demonstrate that they discussed a revised role for the JNA in Bosnia and Herzegovina and they decided that military conscripts born in Bosnia and Herzegovina who were serving in JNA units in Serbia, Montenegro, and Macedonia would be redeployed to Bosnia and Herzegovina. We will present evidence that from January 1992 onwards, there was a convergence and a collaboration between command units and the main Bosnian Serb political party, the Serbian Democratic Party in strategically located Serb-dominated parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the early parts of 1992, we will present evidence showing the increasing control exercised by Serbs over the Territorial Defences in areas characterized by a significant Serb population with the assistance of JNA and forces controlled or linked by -- linked to the Ministry of the Interior from Serbia. By now the Bosnian Serb strategic goals announced officially at the 16th Session of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly on 12 May 1992 are infamous. They clearly set out six goals essential to creating ultimately the goal of Greater Serbia. First: Separate the Serbian people from the two other national communities; second, establish a corridor between Semberija and Krajina; three, establish a corridor in the Drina Valley, thus eliminating the Drina as a border separating Serbian states; four, establish a border on the Una and Neretva rivers; five, divide the city of Sarajevo; and six, establish access to the sea. Radovan Karadzic led the Bosnian Serb leadership to form their own entity and go to war. His six principles would, if achieved, create an independent republic that could eventually rejoin the rump Yugoslav state. Unstated but essential to the achievement of his geopolitical goals was the acquiescence of Muslim and Croat leadership in Bosnia and Herzegovina. A further unstated aim implicit in these goals was that the new state must be almost purely Serbs. This can only be their objective when you consider what the evidence will show that in a systematic way the Bosnian Serbs carried out ethnic cleansing. When Seselj talked about pursuing a Greater Serbia, other members of Bosnian and Serb leadership who agreed with that goal did not use the same language. Slobodan Milosevic insisted that Serbs remain in one state, and he said that the divisions of Yugoslavia into several states which would separate Serbian people and force them to live in separate sovereign states would be out of the question. Officially, Milosevic seemed to have been in favour of the old Yugoslavia during parts of 1991. For Seselj this federal state was only an interim solution in his struggle for a Greater Serbia. We will bring evidence such as this panel discussion with Tanjug's guests, where he's being interviewed and discussing his concept of Greater Serbia and how to achieve that by bringing together populations of Serbs separated by political borders. However, by 1991 Milosevic and the Serbian and Montenegrin members of the socialist Presidency were pursuing the creation of a new Serb state more in line with what Seselj had in mind. Borisav Jovic wrote, and we will present his book on the last days of the SFRY, he said that: "By working to destroy and break up Yugoslavia, Croatia and Bosnia themselves are working to create a Greater Serbia." You can see from the map that Slobodan Milosevic's party targeted, that they were pursuing the same territory. Here in this map you can see the autonomous region of the Krajina on number 1; Western Slavonia marked as number 2, the self-declared Autonomous Region of Western Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem; number 4, the Posavina corridor. The curved line farther to the west is indicated in the text as the optimal western borders of the Serbian counties there, of course the line that Seselj preached Karlobag, Karlovac and Virovitica. As can be seen from the maps used by Milosevic's party his goals in relation to a new Serbian state and Seselj's Greater Serbia cover basically the same territory. The evidence will show that the political and military leadership in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina were fully in line with Milosevic as well as Seselj's notion of creating a Serb state dominated by Serbs out of territory held by Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. As we've discussed already, the evidence will show that Serb leaders in the self-declared regions of Croatia in collaboration with people in Belgrade and Bosnia and Herzegovina set up the necessary political, police, and military structures that later engaged in a war for territory to create the western borders of the new state. Seselj was personally present in those territories from beginning to end. He was present when on July 25, 1990, in Knin -- near Knin, I'm sorry, Milan Babic and other Krajina leaders established a Serb Assembly and the Serbian National Council and passed a declaration on the sovereign and autonomous -- on the sovereignty and autonomy of the Serb nation in Croatia. Seselj was present in the first clashes of violence in the self-declared Autonomous Region in Krajina in March 1991. Seselj's men were involved in the violence in Borovo Selo, in Eastern Slavonia, Seselj was present at Vukovar before it fell to the Serb forces, and also in Vocin. The evidence will show that he was in constant contact with the Croatian Serb leaderships in all of the self-declared autonomous regions, he even supported Milan Babic by the end of 1991 in his opposition to the Vance Plan which proposed peace for the Croatian territories that had been agreed upon by Slobodan Milosevic, Tudjman, and General Kadijevic to allow international forces to come in. The documentary evidence that we will present will demonstrate the high degree of coordination throughout that region that can only mean that the political and military leaders were working together in concert to pursue their common goal. Originally or initially the military leadership was opposed to the disintegration of Yugoslavia, and the evidence shows that they were not in favour of a new Serbian state, but rather pursued the continuation of the old Yugoslavia. However, in July 1991 the evidence will show that the generals, pressured by Milosevic and other leaders of the Presidency, gave up the idea of a unitary Yugoslavia and moved their forces to the future borders of a new Serb state along the lines of the western border I have shown you. When the Serbian and Montenegrin leadership took over the Presidency and thus the Supreme Command of the JNA on the 1st of October, 1991, the evidence will show that the JNA sided with the Serb leadership and warned the Croatian government and other organs that they would retaliate for any military action. The date of 1st October is significant because of so many steps taken throughout the region. The Montenegrin leadership acted in coordination and mobilised their special police unit for the attack on Dubrovnik which started the following day, and the SRS acted on orders of Seselj as well. They established a War Staff on October 1st, changed the name of their Crisis Staff, and Seselj with his associates were already fully cooperating with the JNA and continued to transfer their volunteers into combat. The goal of creating a Greater Serbia was not achieved, but they did achieve ethnic cleansing. We will hear from demographic experts about the changes in Croatia that left the claimed areas basically free of non-Serbs and, in particular, Croats. Seselj himself said on 6 March 1992 in a television interview in Belgrade that he was of the opinion that: "We did not manage to achieve that ideal western border of ours: Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica. We did not succeed with Karlobag but we are somewhere in the vicinity of the former Maslenicki bridge and that is several kilometres away from Karlobag. We did not succeed with Ogulin, however we are close to Ogulin. We did not succeed with Karlovac, however we are holding the suburbs of Karlovac. We did not succeed with Virovitica, but we are holding the suburbs of Pakrac, one part of Pakrac and parts of Western Slavonia." By the end of 1991, the Republika Srpska -- I'm sorry. The -- by the end of 1991, the military and political situation on the ground caused the focus of the JCE to shift to Bosnia and Herzegovina.
