In a conference organized by the Rump Presidency in Belgrade on 3 January 1992 with representatives of the leadership of the self-declared autonomous regions in Croatia, the Bosnian Serbs and the members of the SRS as well as other parties revised the map of targeted areas. In 1992 we have the Epoha map. In January 9 1992 the Bosnian Serb Assembly proclaimed the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In relation to its territories, it stated that it included "areas where the Serbian people are a minority because of the genocide conducted against it in the Second World War." This terminology is very similar to that used by Seselj when he refers to Serbian graves marking the borders of Greater Serbia. The evidence will show that throughout the indictment period, Seselj and the Bosnian Serb leadership pursued basically the same goals in relation to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Seselj continued to have contact with Bosnian Serb leaders throughout the indictment period and even supported them in 1993 in their opposition to Slobodan Milosevic regarding the Vance-Owen Plan, which was a peace proposal for Bosnia and Herzegovina that would have divided the country into ten different ethnic zones. For example, in a speech he gave on March 11, 1993, Seselj said: "We believe that no one has the right to accept the Vance-Owen ultimatum in the name of the Serbian people concerning the internal borders in the territory of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina. Particularly, we believe that one has the right to give the corridor between the Bosnian Krajina and Semberija to the Croats, Muslims, or UNPROFOR in the name of the Serbian people. The Serbian Radical Party maintains its position that the only just and firm boundary determination in the territory of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina can be at the front lines reached." Over this issue Seselj finally split with Slobodan Milosevic, at least temporarily. It is at that point that the indictment period here closes. It was clear from the utterances of the Bosnian Serb leadership that if the Muslims persisted in their attempt to have a state, a unified state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that they faced extinction.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me take a moment to get his words. I had planned to show you a tape, but it's escaping me. "This is the road that you want Bosnia and Herzegovina to take, the same highway of hell and suffering that Slovenia and Croatia went through. Don't you think you won't take Bosnia and Herzegovina to hell and Muslim people to possible extinction." Seselj's view regarding the ethnic diversity of his Greater Serbia was the same. He advocated that ethnic minorities should not exceed more than 8 per cent of the total population. In chapter 10 of his book on the Philippics of Chetnik's Vojvoda, under the headline: "At treatment of non-Serbs in the process of unification is a particular issue ..." Seselj described what he thought should be the role or the place of non-Serb populations in his new Serb state.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you reading slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: He said: "That is inevitable formation of a civilian state, the state of the Serbs equal (loyalty is implicit) citizens, members of other nations, ethnic minorities, and groups. If such state is formed, other nations, ethnic minorities, and groups should not exceed more than 8 per cent of total population; they should not exceed the said percentage in any larger settlement, region, or administrative unit, and there should be no possibility to change their percentage through birth rate." This compelled the resettlement of huge numbers of non-Serbs. The ethnic division on the ground that Karadzic and Seselj requested necessarily meant expulsion of non-Serbs from the claimed territories. Even in territories dominated by the Serbs, Muslims, and Croat settlements had to be uprooted and the non-Serbs driven out in order to ensure a homogenous territory. I think we've been at it another hour, and if it suits the Bench, I think it's appropriate to take a break for the sake of the interpreters. I have an overview of the crime bases and a demonstration of the ethnic recomposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's up to you to decide. We can have a break now or at 20 past 12.00, as you please.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Well, I think we should after an hour take a break then, now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have resumed our hearing. Mrs. Dahl, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First I want to correct a mistake that I made in displaying a photograph, an earlier picture depicting the wrong individual. I want to now display the correct photograph of Milan Lancuzanin, known as Kameni. Now I will return to the objectives of achieving a Greater Serbia. We will present evidence that in Bosnia and Herzegovina before the war there was a mosaic of ethnically diverse communities. I'm sorry, I'm waiting for the computer system to catch up with me. As you can see by this map, it's very colourful. It shows Croats, Muslims, and Serbs almost in a patchwork quilt sharing communities and living together. The next demographic information that the Office of the Prosecution has comes from after the war when things began to be normalised, and you can see by comparison in 1997 our expert demographer will show you that -- that the patchwork is gone, and again waiting for the computer to display the picture. Ethnic cleansing achieved a wholesale reorganization, putting populations into homogeneous areas, and when we looked at this map and built the legend, we didn't even need as many colours or categories. The mixed communities, the beautiful diversity, the inclusiveness of the cultures had been destroyed. I've already mentioned the speech of Radovan Karadzic on 12 May 1992, stressing the crucial importance of taking control of strategic territories. The crime scenes included in this case illustrate the pursuit of those strategic locations. Planning at high-level institutions of the -- at the highest level of military and political leadership can only be the reason that the Bosnian Serbs were able to strategically and methodically select targets to execute their military operations. Here you can see Bosanski Samac, Brcko, and Bijeljina. We will lead limited evidence on this to show the pattern of the attacks and the execution of the overall criminal enterprise. These three municipalities are situated on the Posavina corridor. Before the war, the majority population in Bosanski Samac was of Croatian ethnicity, Brcko had a Muslim majority, and in Bijeljina the majority was Serb. From 1992 onwards, non-Serbs were expelled from these municipalities by force. The evidence we lead will show that the attacks on the non-Serb populations in Bosnia and Herzegovina, starting in Bijeljina, reveal a pattern of crimes that unfortunately, and to the world's horror, was replicated throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina. In these three municipalities, the local authorities as well as the Bosnian Serb leadership asked the SRS to send volunteers to these municipalities. For example, Biljana Plavsic, for instance, wrote letters to Seselj, to Arkan, and to another fellow Mirko Jovic asking for help. Seselj responded. His volunteers arrived and participated in the initial attack on these locations and the crimes that followed. The SRS War Staff sent volunteers led by a fellow named Debeli to Bosanski Samac. In Brcko and Bijeljina, Mirko Blagojevic was in charge of the Radical Party volunteers. The Radical Party volunteers fought alongside the JNA units, the Bosnian Serb Territorial Defence, members of the Serbian MUP, and Arkan's Tigers. The Prosecution will supply evidence that Seselj was informed of these violent attacks and violent events, and in the face of that he promoted the Radical Party commanders involved. For example, under item 15 in the promotion order, Srecko Radovanovic is mentioned as a Chetnik colonel who organized and trained Chetnik units. He is recognised for having been involved in various areas in Croatia and in April 1992 he was constantly in the field of, among other places, Samac and Brcko. Similarly, about Mirko Blagojevic, the remarks include that he spreads the Serbian Chetnik Movement throughout Semberija and commanded Chetnik units in, among other locations, Bijeljina, Zvornik, and Brcko. The catalysts that brought war to Slovenia and Croatia, the paranoia, ethnic referendums, covert arming, the formations of paramilitaries, and ethnic cleansing, came home to Bosnia in the first week of April. Bijeljina was an ethnically divided town of about 36.000 people. It sat or sits 15 kilometres from the Serbian border at the junction of two important roads. The town was the key to the Serb-proclaimed Semberija and Majevica Autonomous Region, and there had been substantial efforts by the SDS to make its police force Serb. Seselj's men were there and participated in the take-over of Bijeljina, which served strategic goals numbers 1, 2, and 3. Reports by the Bosnian Serb police indicate clearly that Seselj's volunteers were involved in crimes before, during, and after the take-over of Bijeljina. In 1993, Seselj promoted Blagojevic to the rank of Vojvoda because of his participation in Bijeljina. The pattern played out again in Zvornik. In April 1992 Zvornik was a town of about 15.000 people, 60 per cent of whom were Muslims. It's nestled on the west bank of the Drina River. A two-lane bridge connected it with the even smaller town of Mali Zvornik on the opposite bank of the river in Serbia. After the referendum for independence, inter-ethnic violence came to Zvornik. On 16 March Zvornik's Serbs proclaimed their own independent Serbian municipality of Zvornik. By the end of March, the police force had split into two rival bands, and by the republic's declaration of independence on 6 April, emotions had reached a fevered pitch. The Serb forces that rose to attack Zvornik were a hodgepodge of professional and ultranationalist troops, including elements of the Zvornik Territorial Defence, Arkan's unit, Seselj's men, and the special operations unit from the Serbian state security. Included were also JNA regular troops, all supported by JNA artillery fire. The first fighting broke out in and around Zvornik in April 8, and the JNA artillery blatantly began shelling Zvornik from inside Serbia on the far side of the river. Arkan arrived that evening and delivered an ultimatum, ordering the Muslims of Zvornik municipality to hand over their arms by the following morning or experience the fate of Bijeljina. Serb forces surrounded the town, and minutes after the ultimatum expired, they attacked. Within hours they had occupied the town. Muslim resistance ceased by nightfall. Seselj himself later bragged about the effectiveness of the elite units. What happened next can only be described as horrifying. Frankly, my concern is in this trial that the more we see of the violence, massacres, deportations, refugee lines, the more we see of the destruction of mosques and churches, the less we see of it, that we will be numbed to these horrors. And as we present this evidence I hope that it remains fresh and compelling and that it is able to continue, as it should, shock humanity. After the Serb forces established control in Zvornik, the non-Serb population, mostly men, were arrested. They were taken to detention facilities. Now, calling them detention facilities makes them seem like maybe they were actually prisons, but they were converted civilian buildings, technical school, the Drinjaca Dom Kulture, a slaughter-house. People detained in these detention facilities were subjected to unsanitary and cruel conditions. They were not provided with adequate food, their detention was arbitrary, it was not in connection with any criminal proceedings, they were forced to work. Thousands of people, mostly Muslims, were expelled from the municipality. We will present evidence that their homes were looted and destroyed, and that Serb forces destroyed religious and cultural monuments. With respect to the crimes that took place in Zvornik, the Prosecution will bring you evidence of the massacre of Muslim men at the Drinjaca Dom Kulture between 30 and 31 May 1992. The murder of 150 men at the Karakaj technical school in the first week of June, the massacre of 150 Muslim men at Gero's slaughter-house in the same week, and the murder of an additional 40 non-Serb detainees during the month of June at the Celopek Dom Kulture. These figures defy imagination. They reflect the extraordinary brutally inflicted on populations in the municipality of Zvornik because they were not Serb. The road leads to Seselj. We will present evidence that in March 1992, while Bosnian Serbs were preparing the attack, Seselj gave a speech in Mali Zvornik, across the river. He declared: "Dear Chetnik brothers, especially you across the Drina River, you are the bravest ones. We are going to clean Bosnia of pagans and show them a road which will take them to the east, where they belong." Zvornik president of the Crisis Staff, Branko Grujic, in April 1992, asked the SRS in Belgrade to send volunteers. Seselj personally approved this request. We will hear evidence that the Radical Party leaders brought volunteers from Loznica commanded by Dragan - I'm just stumbling sometimes with the spellings, I'm sorry - Cvetinovic to Zvornik. When the war broke out, local Serbs joined the volunteers in Zvornik. They fought together, and afterwards Seselj promoted them. The Prosecution will show evidence that the Seselj volunteers took part in the mass killings, in brutalizing the detainees in the various detention facilities, and also forced people to help them loot. Many witnesses will also refer to crimes committed by the Yellow Wasps. The Prosecution will bring evidence that the so-called Yellow Wasps, led by Repic and Zuco Vuckovic were Seselj's volunteers. They had joined the SRS in 1991 and were indoctrinated by Seselj's hate propaganda. They had fought already in Croatia, and SRS headquarters in Belgrade sent them to Zvornik. Throughout the fighting and persecution campaign in Zvornik, Seselj was regularly provided with information by his associates, and we will demonstrate that some of the proceeds from the looting went to fund the Radical Party. The pattern repeated in Bosanski Samac, in Brcko, following the pursuit of the strategic goals of the Bosnian Serbs, and I want to turn to Mostar and Nevesinje. They are located in southern Bosnia and Herzegovina. Those municipalities were relevant to several of the strategic goals of the Bosnian Serbs, namely, the Drina corridor, the border on the rivers Una and Neretva, and access to the sea. In addition, Mostar was of importance because it had two large military barracks, an airport and other military facilities. There was a boy living in a small village in the Nevesinje municipality, whose world collapsed in June 1992. His family was not involved in politics, they felt safe there. Nevesinje was a municipality with a majority Serb control, was already firmly under the control of Serb forces. They felt safe, even when other people started hiding in the woods and fleeing. This boy's family was among the last to leave in June 1992, when they realised that Muslims were not safe in Nevesinje, that innocent civilians were being killed, houses destroyed, villages levelled. This boy fled with his parents, grandparents, siblings, and his extended family. They tried to flee to Mostar, but they were captured by Serb soldiers who took them to what qualified as a detention facility in a village of Zijemlje. There the terrified children saw their relatives being beaten and tortured. These children were separated from their parents and grandparents and they never saw them again. Their bodies were found in a pit. They moved from one detention location to another. After about two weeks, this small group of terrified children and two old women were taken off -- taken in the direction of Stolac and dropped off by Serb soldiers in the middle of nowhere. Croat soldiers rescued them. This boy lost his parents and grandparents and grew up in a children's home. His experience brings home the human suffering in Nevesinje and Mostar. We will present evidence from victims, soldiers, and experts about the mass murders committed in this vicinity in June 1992. 88 Muslim civilians were murdered at the Ubarak city dump in Mostar on June 13th; 18 non-Serb civilians were murdered at the city mortuary in Sutina in Mostar; more than 70 Muslim civilians that were captured when they were fleeing from Nevesinje on June 22 were murdered, among them many women, children, and elderly. Two women detained and assaulted at Boracko Jezero were also murdered. Finally, the Prosecution will also provide other evidence of the Serb forces, including sexual assault. Seselj is responsible for these crimes. According to the evidence the Prosecution will lead, before the war, neither the Radical Party nor the Chetnik movement had a noticeable presence in Mostar. In neighbouring Nevesinje, Arsen Grahovac promoted the Serbian Chetnik ideology. His pub became a gathering point for the movement, Radical Party members and sympathizers. Grahovac established a unit called Karadjordje which set up roadblocks, harassed the local non-Serb population, and set off explosives in several Muslim-owned properties in Nevesinje as early as 1991. This unit was comprised of between 80 and 100 members and sympathizers of the Serbian Chetnik Movement and the Serbian Radical Party and they operated both in Mostar and Nevesinje. The group commanded by Grahovac was not the only group of volunteers associated with Seselj. From autumn 1991 and particularly 1992 Seselj's volunteers from Serbia and Montenegro and from the battle-fields in Croatia arrived. The Radical Party and Chetnik volunteers were commanded by Branislav Vakic and Radovan Radovic. In May 1992 Mostar was taken over by Serb forces comprised of the JNA, the Serbian Territorial Defence, Serbian Radical Party volunteers, and Red Berets from the Serbian DB in an offensive commanded by General Perisic. We will hear from participants in the attack that Oliver Baret, one of the leading Radical Party commanders with close connections to the Radical Party leadership, arrived from Belgrade and was present in the military headquarters of the JNA in Mostar. While there, he kept in communication with the Radical Party volunteers who participated in the offensive. In every murder and abuse I have mentioned in both Mostar and in Nevesinje, Radical Party and Chetnik volunteers were involved, again following the pattern: Seselj visited the conflict area, and again, promoted those commanders involved in the crimes. Vakic received a promotion in connection with Vukovar as well. Radovic and Oliver Baret were promoted to Vojvoda in 1994. I want to turn to Sarajevo now. Sarajevo is the fifth strategic goal of the Bosnian Serbs, that is the division of the city. In April and May of 1992, Serb forces including Radical Party volunteers attacked and took control of municipalities or parts of the municipalities in the area that comprised Greater Sarajevo. We will hear from witnesses that following the take-over there Serb forces conducted a persecution campaign against the non-Serbs, here mostly Muslims. The crimes included in this indictment include the Ilijas municipality and the Vogosca municipality. In late 1991 and early 1992, Serbs in the Greater Sarajevo area took steps to establish control over several of these areas. Ratko Adzic, who was president of the SDS party, became the head of the Serb Crisis Staff and Territorial Defence in Ilijas. At the end of April 1992, Serbs from Ilijas took over the police station and fired all the Muslim and Croat policemen. Muslims and Croats tried unsuccessfully to set up their own police station nearby, but the Serb police seized all the ammunition and left them defenseless. Vasilje Vidovic was one of Seselj's volunteers who came from Ilijas. He had been with the SRS in Knin and now returned with about 20 men to Ilijas. He was a member of Ratko Adzic's staff and he was known for his brutality. He drew -- he drove a car with a human skull fixed on the front of it. Outside the house where he lived were displayed two human heads on poles. Serb forces attacked on the night between 4th and 5th of June, 1992, and the evidence will show that Vidovic's men, local policemen, and other armed men belonging to the Territorial Defence entered the town and committed crimes. People were detained following the pattern that we've heard in all of the crimes discussed so far, and the evidence will show that Seselj's men detained people, beat them, kicked them, put them on a bus, and detained them in a warehouse for several months before moving them around. We will present detailed evidence that these people were tortured, raped, killed, that prisoners were used from the detention facilities to carry out forced labour, including digging trenches and doing work at the front line. The commander's men, Vasilje Vidovic, murdered 27 detainees in the summer of 1993 as revenge for Serb losses. The pattern was repeated in other neighbourhoods around Sarajevo. Let us turn to Slavko Aleksic. He and his Radical Party volunteers controlled the area of the Jewish cemetery in Grbavica. His unit was called Ravna Gora Chetnik detachment. In 1993 Seselj promoted him to the rank of Vojvoda. The promotion order recognises his active promotion of the ideas of the party and the movement in Sarajevo and identifies him as the commander of the Novo Sarajevo Chetnik detachment. After the war, Seselj publicly praised Aleksic and the SRS volunteers in Grbavica saying that they had performed a great service to the Radical Party and to the cause of Serb nationalism. What did Aleksic do for the Serb cause? He and his men persecuted the non-Serbs in Grbavica, they conducted arbitrary searches of their homes, they looted, they raped, they beat, and they killed. They forced men and women to work under dangerous conditions. More than 80 civilians were killed while performing forced labour. The pattern repeats itself in Ilidza municipality. Branislav Gavrilovic also known as Brne was an active in the Greater Sarajevo area. He became the leader of the Serbian Youth Movement for Bosnia and Herzegovina. An organisation that joined Seselj's Chetnik movement after he met Seselj in Bijeljina in 1991. Seselj later appointed Gavrilovic a volunteer commander in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. On the screen is the certification by Seselj of his command. Gavrilovic was one of the leaders of the SRS party in Ilidza. During the war he was in charge of a large unit of Chetnik volunteers. The Prosecution will provide evidence that Gavrilovic, while in Croatia and later in Bosnia and Herzegovina, would receive orders from the SRS office in Belgrade and would meet with Seselj, both in Belgrade and in Sarajevo. Seselj appointed Gavrilovic a Vojvoda in May 1993. His distinguished service was in Croatia and Sarajevo. What did he do in Sarajevo? We will bring you evidence that on 17 July 1993, Branislav Gavrilovic and his Chetnik volunteers captured four members of the Sarajevo Territorial Defence in their positions on Mount Igman facing Ilidza. They shot one of them, a 17-year-old boy, on the spot. They took the other prisoners downhill to a field where Branislav Gavrilovic and more of his men were waiting. Gavrilovic and one of his subordinates interrogated the prisoners, hit them, beat them, and kicked them. Two of the prisoners were murdered after the interrogation. The crimes I just described were committed by Seselj and other members of the joint criminal enterprise because they pursued the common goal of achieving Serb domination in targeted territories in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Seselj and his associates wanted to expel the Croats and the Muslims. To achieve this, they conducted a persecution campaign for which untold numbers of innocent people of all ages paid a heavy price. This brings me to the close of my presentation this morning. At the close of the case you will judge the evidence that the Prosecution has brought and what defence Mr. Seselj may present and determine whether we have proved to your satisfaction the following charges. There are three counts of crimes against humanity, persecution, deportation and inhumane acts in the form of forcible transfer, and three counts of violations of the laws and customs of war against people, those are murder, torture, and cruel treatment, and three counts of the violation of the laws and customs of war against property, that is, the wanton destruction of villages not justified by military necessity, wilful damage done to institutions dedicated to religion, and plunder. The Prosecution submits that the evidence will show at the end of the case that Mr. Seselj is criminally responsible for these crimes because of what he did. We allege that he planned, instigated, ordered, committed, or otherwise aided and abetted these crimes. The Prosecution submits that Seselj himself committed the crime of persecution by his direct and public denigration in speeches made in Vukovar, Mali Zvornik, and Hrtkovci. And in the counts of deportation and forcible transfer that occurred in connection with his speech in Hrtkovci. Finally, we submit that the law allows Seselj to be held criminally responsible for these crimes because he acted in concert in a joint criminal enterprise, the object of which was the permanent forcible removal of Croat, Muslim, and other non-Serb inhabitants from large areas of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina claimed as Serb territory and that realising this objective necessarily required the commission of crimes. We will present evidence that shows the specific crimes identified in the indictment that were within the objective of the joint criminal enterprise. The indictment alleges that the crimes of deportation and forcible transfer constituted the common objective of the joint criminal enterprise from the outset. The other crimes such as murder, detention, torture, beatings, sexual assaults, and the destruction of property were, at a minimum, foreseeable, if not part of the objective from the outset. The Prosecution will prove that these crimes were adopted by the members of the JCE during the events and incorporated into their criminal plan. The evidence will show that the objective of the joint criminal enterprise never changed, but the methods of the implementation of this common objective evolved and the crimes charged in the indictment became part of the criminal means by which the common goal was pursued between 1991 and 1993. There can be no doubt that these crimes were foreseeable. In Seselj's own words in an interview he gave on 24 May in 1991 after he met with Radovan Karadzic in Bosnia and Herzegovina he said: "We have already deployed several Chetnik groups in Zagreb and other towns across Croatia which are trained in sabotage and terrorist activities. If Serbian civilians start to be massacred, the Chetniks will strike at Zagreb and other concentrations of Croats using their full strength. You know, when one retaliates, revenge is blind. There would be innocent victims but what can you do? Let the Croats think about that first. We shall not strike first, but if they should strike we're not even going to bother where our blows land. Also, unless the army disarms the Ustashas immediately, there will be a lot of blood." In September 1993 Seselj was interviewed again, this time on a radio programme. One of the listeners asked Seselj whether he ever worried about people other than Serbs, noting that an innocent population was suffering due to his views. He answers: "Why would I have a guilty consciousness? So many innocent Serbs suffered in this war and I need to worry about those who belong to another enemy people, if possibly there was an innocent one among them that suffered. You know, in war one experiences great turmoil, great troubles, and I in war above all worry about those who belong to my own people." In closing, I think the root of this evil is a lack of empathy. The evidence will sustain the charges I pray, and that when you judge the Prosecution's case you will find it sound and complete. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Ms. Dahl. Tomorrow, Mr. Seselj, you will be given the floor for your own statement. I make sure that there is absolute equality of arms. Are you going to need this rostrum or the lectern? I was wondering whether you had some water as well. I can't see that. I can't see whether you have any water. So the only technical matter is whether you are going to be on your feet when you make your statement or whether you are going to be seated.

I prepared to speak for four hours and I would like to speak four hours. Thank you.
